title: Dead Letters: The University of Chicago's Classical Philology Journal, the Atom of Evidence, and Who Decides What Sappho Is (EA-MMRS-DL-01)
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: A census of Classical Philology (University of Chicago Press, 1906–2026) on a codebook of reach: at what grain the journal permits the question of what an ancient text is (the locus, the work, the corpus), by what kind of argument, and where the record of the decision is kept. All 4,252 titles coded and audited; the journal's pages of 1906–1930 read whole; its abstracts of 2020–26; GRBS, BMCR and Classical Quarterly compared; conviction verdicts coded for their stated grounds; bylines, masthead and open citations measured; the closed record measured from its metadata. The question is opened at the locus and seldom at the corpus; relations are admitted and used to secure the received whole; decisions about texts are cited less than the journal's other work; and the record of how they are made is the least open of the three journals of the combined audit. The case is Sappho fragment 31: who decides what Sappho is, how the received reading is held, and how the text is liberated, operation by operation. The third station of the combined audit, after Who Speaks for the Classics (#1770) and This Is Not Philosophy (#1773). Version 1.1 (18 November 2026, in place) brings the case of fragment 31 to ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ v3.0 (#1785): three readings and two lines, the jealousy reading as the transmitted reading and the non-jealous erotic reading as the scholarship's strongest, both stopping at the poem's public line, and the gate's verdict as one that kept the public line and declined the account of the form.
content_type: Journal article (Machine-Mediated Reception Studies); working notebook: census, audit and case
substrate: Human–machine collaborative. The census's question, predictions, title, rulings and readings are Lee Sharks's, stated and dated in the text. The harvest, coding, measures, audits and drafting were done in session by Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction; codes were made by parallel Claude readers and the lead instance, and audited by blind readers, as §3 states. The blind title run was made by ChatGPT. Readings by DeepSeek (three) and ChatGPT (one) were checked point by point against the notebook and its files before any was applied. SPXI-treated. By Classical Philology's own rule, the use of generative AI for composition or editing is research misconduct for work submitted to it (§8.2, §11); this census is deposited in the commons with its method and provenance stated.
methodology: Crossref census of the journal (11,206 records; 4,252 articles and notes); title coding on a reach codebook (§2) with verbatim spans machine-checked; a blind parallel run and a blind audit of 200 codes across five bodies (κ 0.78); the journal's public-domain pages of 1906–1930 read whole (EA-CORPORA-40; Internet Archive) with direction and opens-to classes; OpenAlex abstracts of 2020–26; GRBS (1,752 items), BMCR (740 reviews) and Classical Quarterly (779 items) on the same codebook; a conviction lexicon with every sentence read and coded for polarity, object and stated ground; byline concentration and masthead; OpenCitations citations to 991 items with citing venues; the journal's and the Press's stated rules, dated. Files are listed in the text.
falsification_conditions: The figures are falsified if the codes do not rebuild from the stated files against Crossref and the seated pages; if a code's span is absent from its source; if the audit's disagreements, read by grain, are shown to cover the gradient; if the bare verdicts of §8.3 are shown, on the full reviews, to summarize stated arguments at a rate that removes the asymmetry (§9.12); if the citation gap does not survive a further control (venue, citing period) or the canon test shows the deciding items cited in the editions and reference works that carry them (§9.9); or if a canonical name is shown to have been divided at the corpus grain in the bodies read after 1993 beyond the one case recorded. The reading of fragment 31 fails where #1781's own conditions say it fails.

wiki_article: Dead Letters: The University of Chicago's Classical Philology Journal, the Atom of Evidence, and Who Decides What Sappho Is is a working notebook by Lee Sharks, deposited on 17 November 2026 as an article in Machine-Mediated Reception Studies (version 1.0, the notebook at v0.34, SPXI-treated) and the third station of the archive's combined audit of the fields, after Who Speaks for the Classics (#1770) and This Is Not Philosophy (#1773). It is a census of Classical Philology, the University of Chicago Press journal edited in the University of Chicago's Department of Classics since 1906, on a codebook of reach: at what grain the journal permits the question of what an ancient text is, the locus, the work or the corpus, by what kind of argument, and where the record of the decision is kept. All 4,252 of the journal's article and note titles are coded and audited; its public-domain pages of 1906–1930 are read whole; its abstracts of 2020–2026, Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies, Bryn Mawr Classical Review and Classical Quarterly are read on the same codebook. The census finds the question opened at the locus and seldom at the corpus in every body read; relations among parts admitted and used chiefly to secure the received whole; verdicts on a whole mostly given without a stated ground; the journal's decisions about texts cited at less than half the rate of its other work; and its record the least open of the three journals of the audit, with no abstract in the publisher's metadata deposit and 97% of its works classed closed by OpenAlex. Its case is Sappho fragment 31: who decides what Sappho is, how the jealousy reading, supplied in 1724 and written into the text in 1816, is held, and how the text is liberated by a set of operations any reader can perform. It sets the three stations as one machine, in which philosophy places positions on the object and reception widens its content while philology decides it, and it records that by the journal's own rule the census, made with AI, would be research misconduct if submitted to the journal it measures. Version 1.1, reissued in place on 18 November 2026, brings the census's case of Sappho's fragment 31 to version 3.0 of ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ (#1785). It distinguishes the jealousy reading, which transmission delivers, from the scholarship's strongest reading, the non-jealous erotic reading, and finds both stopping at the poem's public line, so that what the journal's verdict kept was the surface and what it declined was the account of the poem's form. It restates the strongest opponent as the erotic reading, differentiates the ethical charge, and sets the editor's chapter 'The Erotics of Again' beside fragment 1's 'again' as the mechanism by which, on the future-reader reading, the poet comes to whoever calls her: a voice made to be called rather than a body performed again.
